lycra.origin: LYCRA is the principal elastane brand of The LYCRA Company, headquartered in the United States; the brand grew out of DuPont's synthetic-fiber business. The generic fiber is spandex (US) or elastane (EU), a segmented polyurethane. Ownership has changed repeatedly: Shandong Ruyi bought the company in January 2019, its lenders took control in 2022, and after a prepackaged Chapter 11 case in 2026 control passed to investment funds that had held the company's debt. Readers should confirm the current owner with the company.
lycra.structure: Spandex is a block copolymer in which long, flexible soft segments (typically polyether or polyester glycols) alternate with short, rigid hard segments formed from an aromatic diisocyanate chain-extended with diols or diamines, giving urethane and urea linkages. The hard segments aggregate into hydrogen-bonded domains that act as physical cross-links, while the soft segments are amorphous and coil above their glass transition. Stretching uncoils the soft segments; the hard domains pull the network back when the load is removed. Filaments are usually coalesced multifilaments.
lycra.process: In the conventional route for spandex, a macroglycol is capped with excess diisocyanate to form a prepolymer, which is chain-extended (commonly with a diamine) in a polar solvent such as dimethylacetamide. The polymer solution is dry-spun: extruded into a heated column where the solvent evaporates and is recovered, and adjacent filaments fuse into a coalesced yarn. Finish is applied and the yarn is wound. Mills then combine it with other fibers by core spinning, covering, air-jet entangling or direct knitting. The LYCRA Company's grade-specific processes are proprietary.
lycra.performance: Spandex can extend several times its length and recover, which is why small percentages transform fit and shape retention. Moisture regain is low. It is degraded by chlorine, prolonged heat, UV and some body oils, which cause loss of recovery over time; chlorine-resistant grades exist. High heat-setting temperatures can damage it, so blends are processed carefully. It takes acid and disperse dyes with variable fastness. Performance claims for particular LYCRA grades are producer statements tied to those grades.
lycra.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: spandex melts and burns with a chemical odor, leaving a soft, sticky residue, and in blends the small elastane fraction is easily masked. Microscopy of stretched fabric can show the fine elastic core or coalesced filaments. FTIR identifies polyurethane; quantitative analysis of blends uses selective dissolution. The word LYCRA is often used loosely for any stretch fabric or for elastane from other producers.
lycra.labeling: LYCRA is a trademark, not a generic name. The FTC rules at 16 CFR 303.7 define spandex as a fiber of at least 85% segmented polyurethane, and because Part 303 incorporates the ISO 2076 names, US labels may use either spandex or elastane; EU labels must use elastane under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. In the US a fiber under 5 percent can generally be grouped as other fiber, but one with clearly established functional significance, as stretch usually is, is named with its percentage. A trademark may appear only alongside the generic name.
lycra.past: Elastane was developed in the mid-twentieth century as a lighter, more durable alternative to rubber thread, and LYCRA became a widely recognized brand of the fiber in foundation garments, swimwear, hosiery and later denim and sportswear. The business passed from DuPont through a series of owners. Shandong Ruyi's 2019 purchase ended in default, and its lenders took control in 2022. On 17 March 2026 The LYCRA Company filed a prepackaged Chapter 11 case in the Southern District of Texas, emerging on 20 May 2026 with more than 1.2 billion dollars of debt eliminated and new equity owners.

kevlar.origin: Kevlar is a para-aramid brand now owned by Arclin, a US chemical company that is a portfolio company of an affiliate of TJC, L.P. DuPont created the brand and sold its Aramids business, including Kevlar and Nomex, to Arclin; the deal was announced on 29 August 2025 and completed on 1 April 2026 at a value of about 1.8 billion dollars. DuPont retained a minority equity stake of about 16% in Arclin. The generic fiber is para-aramid, poly(p-phenylene terephthalamide) (PPTA).
kevlar.structure: PPTA consists of benzene rings joined at their para (1,4) positions through amide linkages, giving a straight, rigid rod-like chain. Hydrogen bonds between amide groups of neighboring chains form sheets, and the sheets stack through aromatic interactions. Because the rigid chains form a liquid-crystalline solution, spinning aligns them almost perfectly along the fiber axis, producing very high crystallinity, a highly oriented fibrillar structure, high tensile strength and modulus, and weak lateral cohesion that makes the fiber prone to splitting and poor in compression.
kevlar.process: In the generally described route, PPTA is made by low-temperature polycondensation of p-phenylenediamine with terephthaloyl chloride in an amide solvent. The polymer is dissolved in concentrated sulfuric acid to form a liquid-crystalline (anisotropic) dope, which is extruded through an air gap into a cold water bath (dry-jet wet spinning). The shear and extension in the gap orient the rod-like domains. The yarn is washed free of acid, neutralized and dried; high-modulus grades are heat-treated under tension. Yarns are then woven, knitted, cut to staple, pulped or used in composites.
kevlar.performance: Para-aramid combines high tensile strength and modulus with low density, which is why it is used in ballistic and cut-resistant products and composites. It does not melt; it decomposes and chars at high temperature and is inherently flame resistant. Weaknesses include degradation under UV light, sensitivity to strong acids and bases, poor compressive strength, and moisture uptake that can affect ballistic panels unless protected. It is difficult to dye and is often solution-dyed. Protective performance depends on the whole tested system.
kevlar.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and unsafe for protective items: para-aramid resists ignition, chars without melting and does not form a bead. Undyed fiber is characteristically yellow-gold. Microscopy shows smooth round filaments that split into fibrils when cut or abraded. FTIR distinguishes para-aramid from meta-aramid and from UHMWPE. Kevlar is often used loosely for any aramid or any cut-resistant fabric.
kevlar.labeling: Kevlar is a trademark, not a generic name. Under the FTC rules at 16 CFR 303.7 aramid is the generic name for fibers of long-chain synthetic polyamide in which at least 85% of the amide linkages attach directly to two aromatic rings; EU labels must use aramid under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. For protective equipment, fiber labeling is separate from performance certification, which depends on the relevant product standard and tested configuration.
kevlar.past: Kevlar came from DuPont's research into aromatic polyamides that form liquid-crystalline solutions, a discovery that allowed rigid-chain polymers to be spun into highly oriented fiber. DuPont commercialized it for tire reinforcement, body armor, ropes, composites and protective gloves, and the name became closely associated with DuPont for decades. In August 2025 DuPont agreed to sell the Aramids business, which had about 1,900 employees, five manufacturing sites and 2024 net sales of about 1.3 billion dollars, to Arclin. The sale closed on 1 April 2026.
